item.title: Astrolight delivers first space-to-ground laser communication link to client
item.description: WARSAW, Poland — The Lithuanian space startup Astrolight has announced the successful commissioning of a space-to-ground laser communication link. The link company’s ATLAS-1 laser communication terminal aboard ERMIS-3, an 8U cubesat led by the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens as part of the ERMIS mission, connected with HolOGS-1, the optical ground station of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece.

item.title: The U.S. already oversees commercial space. Novelty is not a regulatory gap.
item.description: A voluntary federal pilot could determine whether America’s next generation of commercial-space businesses operates under clear, generally applicable rules or must first obtain discretionary government permission merely because an activity is new. The Office of Space Commerce’s new Space Commerce Certification (SCC) pilot program may help coordinate novel proposals, but it could become the basis for, or evolve into, an informal permission system if policymakers misinterpret Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty as requiring a bespoke authorization and supervision regime whenever a commercial mission is unfamiliar. Article VI requires states to authorize and continuously supervise nongovernmental activities in outer space, but leaves each state to determine the domestic form, intensity and timing of those functions; it neither requires mission-specific approval because an activity is novel nor compels a customized federal supervisory regime for each unfamiliar use of a spacecraft.

item.title: Rockets are scaling faster than the infrastructure beneath them
item.description: Western launch capacity is usually discussed in terms of rockets: how many, how reusable, how cheap. Those questions still matter, but they are increasingly not the ones setting the pace. In 2021, 36 rockets launched from Cape Canaveral . Last year it was 110, with another 65 from Vandenberg, and the Space Force has said the two ranges could see up to 3,000 launches a year by 2036. Much of that growth has run through ground infrastructure built decades ago. As reusable rockets start to behave more like transportation assets, the infrastructure beneath them will need to make the same transition.
